text: Writing a useful program is half the work. The other half is getting it onto someone's computer - built for their machine, signed so they can trust it, kept up to date - and that half is usually done badly, or copied from the last project and done badly again.

heading: The same five hundred lines, again
text: Two of our own tools carry nearly identical delivery machinery: cut a release, build it for two kinds of processor, prove where it was built, install it on six systems to see it works, and publish a signed package repository. Each copy drifts. A fix made in one never reaches the other. And the next project starts by copying the newest one - including its mistakes.

heading: One conveyor, called, not copied
text: The conveyor does the delivering once, for everyone. A project keeps one short declaration - its name, how its releases are named, which systems it ships to, which key signs it - and calls the conveyor at a pinned version. Improving the conveyor improves every project that moves to the new version, and none of them is changed by surprise.

heading: Like a postal service
text: Nobody builds their own mail van to send a letter. You write the address clearly and hand it over; the service knows the roads.

heading: What the machines actually run
text: It ships what our machines use: Arch Linux packages for the lab and desktops, Alpine packages for postmarketOS phones - from one declaration, each with a signed repository. Other systems join when someone needs them.

heading: What it does not do
text: It does not decide when a project releases or what its version is: that stays with each language's own tool. It cannot make a broken program work - it can only refuse to publish one that fails its checks.

heading: Where it stands
text: Designed, from the delivery machinery of snapall and lab-agent. The first step is to move both onto it with nothing visible changing for anyone who installed them; then Alpine packages, and the phone's shell as their first user.
